entities.name: Jamshīd al-Kāshī
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ghiyāth al-Dīn Jamshīd Masʿūd al-Kāshī, born in Kashan, Persia, around 1380, was a towering polymath of the Timurid Renaissance, whose astronomical and mathematical innovations profoundly advanced calculation and observation in the Islamic world during the early 15th century. Operating primarily from the vibrant intellectual hub of Samarkand under the patronage of Ulugh Beg, al-Kāshī's work transcended mere theoretical inquiry, laying practical foundations for more precise astronomical tables and trigonometric functions that would influence subsequent generations of scholars. His contributions are critical for understanding the sophistication of medieval Islamic science and its transmission to later traditions, positioning him as a key figure in the pre-modern scientific landscape.

Al-Kāshī's most celebrated mathematical achievement was the calculation of pi to 16 decimal places (or 9 sexagesimal places), a record that stood for over a century and a half. He developed highly accurate sine and tangent tables, notably in his *Risāla al-Watar wa’l-Jayb* (Treatise on the Chord and Sine), and authored *Miftāḥ al-Ḥisāb* (Key of Arithmetic), a comprehensive textbook that introduced decimal fractions to a wider audience, facilitating complex calculations without cumbersome sexagesimal systems. In astronomy, his *Zīj-i Khāqānī* (The Khāqānī Astronomical Tables) improved upon earlier works by Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, providing new methods for determining planetary longitudes and solar eclipses, and he also invented the Plate of Conjunctions and the Sphere of Sizes to aid astronomical computations.

entities.summary:
Ghiyāth al-Dīn Jamshīd Masʿūd al-Kāshī, a towering figure in medieval Islamic mathematics and astronomy, emerged from Kashan, Persia, around 1380, reaching his zenith under the patronage of Ulugh Beg in Samarkand. His intellectual contributions, spanning the early 15th century, fundamentally advanced numerical computation, spherical astronomy, and the precise determination of astronomical constants, marking a high point in the scientific golden age that flourished across the Timurid Empire. Al-Kāshī's work transcended mere refinement, introducing novel algorithms and computational methods that pushed the boundaries of accuracy in a pre-calculus era, solidifying his reputation as one of the era's most formidable mathematical minds.

Al-Kāshī's most celebrated achievement includes the calculation of pi to 16 decimal places (or 17 sexagesimal places) in his treatise *Risāla al-Muḥīṭiyya* (The Treatise on the Circumference) in 1424, a level of precision unsurpassed for nearly two centuries. He also developed a sophisticated method for computing sine of one degree, known as the 'Chord of One Degree' method, which involved solving a cubic equation and demonstrating an early form of iteration. His monumental work, *Miftāḥ al-Ḥisāb* (The Key to Arithmetic), compiled around 1427, served as a comprehensive textbook, systematizing arithmetic for integers, fractions, and sexagesimal numbers, and presenting methods for root extraction and the summation of series. Furthermore, at the Samarkand observatory, he designed the *Plate of Conjunctions*, a mechanical analog computer capable of solving planetary position problems.
